extracted.intended_audience: aspiring fiction writers (beginners through intermediate) seeking craft and publishing advice
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance on writing fiction (craft, drafting, research, workshops) and on submitting/querying for publication and representation. Emphasizes priorities for producing a workable first draft, using research sparingly, handling critiques, and professional submission practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: The story always comes first / 'story belongs in front'
rubrics_metrics.description: Prioritize the story itself over exhaustive research or background detail; the narrative must drive the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: King: "On the whole, I think story belongs in front..." Research/back-story should serve the story, not replace it. Remember you are writing a novel (or story), not a research paper. Keep the essential narrative and themes primary; use research only to enhance rather than to dictate plot or pacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use research sparingly for verisimilitude ('a handful of spices')
rubrics_metrics.description: When you must step away from 'write what you know', do targeted research to supply a touch of realism—enough to produce verisimilitude but not so much that it overwhelms the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research is 'back story'—the key word is back. Use it like spices in a sauce: a few correct details will finish the story and reduce letters from picky readers. Avoid letting the 'tail wag the dog'—do not let research or procedural detail become the story itself. Example: King made up police details while writing the first draft and later did ridealongs to correct 'howlers.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Write with the door shut (write for yourself / the Ideal Reader)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compose initial drafts alone, writing for your own sensibility or an imagined Ideal Reader rather than to please or preempt critics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: King's formulation: 'I could do that because I was writing with the door shut—writing only for myself and the Ideal Reader in my mind.' This allows liberties (making up unknown facts) and preserves creative momentum. Avoid early self-censoring to placate workshop expectations or potential nitpickers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid frequent public critiques while drafting (don't write with the door open)
rubrics_metrics.description: Daily or immediate critiques (workshopping every draft aloud) tend to force explanations and second-guessing, which can harm the creative flow and the shape of a first draft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: King argues that many workshop comments are vague and non-actionable (e.g., 'I loved the feeling...it had something...'), and that daily critique pressures writers to explain and justify choices. Workshops can be intellectually stimulating and useful for networking or when skillfully run, but they often cause the 'I hafta' pressure and can lead to writer's block. Consider keeping early drafts private and seeking focused, specific feedback later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get the first draft down quickly; protect the creative shape
rubrics_metrics.description: Write the first draft while the form is clear in your head—don't interrupt the flow with frequent explanations, defenses, or excessive tinkering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: King: 'what you should probably be doing is writing as fast as the Gingerbread Man runs, getting that first draft down on paper while the shape of the fossil is still bright and clear in your mind.' Preserve momentum; avoid over-analysis during initial drafting so that the shape of the work isn't lost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critiques must be specific and actionable to be useful
rubrics_metrics.description: Vague praise or non-specific observations ('I loved the imagery', 'it had a sense of...') are of limited use when revising; helpful critique should address language, narrative sense, and concrete problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: King complains that many workshop comments fail to touch language or narrative sense. Seek or cultivate feedback that points to specific sentences, scenes, structural issues, or inconsistencies rather than nebulous impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing classes and seminars: no magic, but some benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Classes won't give you a 'secret ingredient' but can be valuable because they treat your desire to write seriously, provide teaching from experienced writers, and sometimes create business contacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: King is skeptical that classes are a silver bullet, but acknowledges advantages: discipline, validation, the opportunity to meet veteran writers, and potential contacts (e.g., agents). Decide based on your personality and whether the class will help rather than stifle your process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn by reading a lot and writing a lot; most lessons are self-taught
rubrics_metrics.description: The most valuable learning comes from sustained reading and regular writing practice rather than dependence on formal instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: King: 'You learn best by reading a lot and writing a lot, and the most valuable lessons of all are the ones you teach yourself.' Emphasize practice and wide reading as primary training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read the market before submitting
rubrics_metrics.description: Familiarize yourself with the magazines and publishers that print the kind of work you write—formats, tone, typical lengths, and editorial preferences—before sending submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the magazines themselves, writer's journals, Writer's Market, and LMP to learn where your work might fit. King: 'Submitting stories without first reading the market is like playing darts in a dark room.' Thumbnail descriptions help but are no substitute for actually reading the market's content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good presentation matters (submission formatting and cover letter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Present your manuscript professionally: a brief cover letter, list of prior publications, good-quality white bond paper, double-spaced copy, address in upper-left, phone number, and approximate word count in the upper-right of the first page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: King relays Frank's checklist: keep the cover letter brief (mention where you've published and a line or two about what the piece is about), thank the editor for reading, use proper paper (no 'slippery erasable stuff'), double-space, and be honest about word count. Editors can tell length by riffling pages; presentation makes it easier for editors to try to like your work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep careful records of submissions and contacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Track where you've submitted each piece, the responses received, and any personal contacts or notes about each market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frank keeps a detailed record of stories making the rounds, responses, and magazines where personal contact exists (even minor). This helps manage re-submissions, avoid duplicate submissions to closed markets, and exploit networking opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have an agent if your work is salable — but vet agents carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: If your work is marketable, seek literary representation; agents can open doors, but not all agents are ethical or competent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: King: 'You should have an agent, and if your work is salable, you will have only a moderate amount of trouble finding one.' However, ask agents for 'bona fides' (publishers/magazines they've sold to), beware agents who charge reading fees or promise miracles, and be cautious of anyone soliciting with only an ad. Consider the agent's track record before signing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Query strategy and what to include in agent queries
rubrics_metrics.description: Write a literate, concise query letter that lists your publication credits and any awards, mentions the project in a line or two, and offers sample material (stories or opening pages) if requested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: King gives Frank's successful template: a brief salutation, list of published stories with venues and payments where relevant, a one-line description of the novel/project, an offer to send sample material, and a courteous close. Including a prize or reputable credits can be persuasive. Provide contact information (address and phone) and be prepared to send the first eighty pages if requested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be your own advocate; be canny, careful, and assiduous
rubrics_metrics.description: Search for agents/publishers proactively using resources (Writer's Market, LMP), tailor queries, and approach agent hunting with care and diligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: King: 'You must begin as your own advocate.' Investigate agents, circle compatible names from market listings, and send thoughtful, targeted queries rather than mass mailings. Recognize the difference between legitimate agents and unscrupulous operators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary of agents who promise to read for a fee; consider alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Agents who charge reading fees are suspect—some reputable agencies have charged fees historically, but many fee-charging agents are unscrupulous; if desperate, vanity presses are an alternative that at least gives the writer something for the money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: King cautions skepticism: while a few fee-reading agencies once existed, 'all too many are unscrupulous fucks.' If you are that anxious to be published and considering paying, be realistic about the tradeoffs and verify the agent's bona fides before paying.
